Simple Present vs Simple Past to Contrast Events in Different Times
You use the simple present to talk about things that usually happen or actions that you frequently do, while the simple past is used to express actions that started and finished in the past.

When you express general truths and events that happen in the present we use the simple present tense. With this tense, we can include a time expression to specify the information, for example every day, every week, once a month, every year, once a week.

Don’t forget that for the subject pronouns I, we, you and they, the simple present form is the same as the base form of the verb and for the negative and interrogative form the auxiliary verb is do. For the pronouns she, he or it you need to add s and es, and you need the auxiliary does for the negative and interrogative form.


Examples:
They design a new program.
They don´t design a new program.
Do they design a new program?

The company designs software every day.
He doesn't design software.
Does Pedro design software?

On the other hand, you use the simple past tense to talk about a complete event in the past. You can form the simple past tense by adding ed, -ied to the verb when the verb is regular. For irregular verbs, however, you have to learn how they change. There are some specific time expressions you can use with this tense, for example yesterday, last month, and two years ago.


Examples:
We designed a new program yesterday. (regular verb)
They studied in this institution last year. (regular verb)
He found new software 5 years ago. (irregular verb)

You need the auxiliary verb did for the negative and interrogative form, for all the subject pronouns.

Examples:
We didn´t design a new program.
Did they study here?
He didn´t find the program.

Don't forget to keep the verb in its base form in both negative and interrogative sentences.
Did you prepare your part on values and types?
Why do you ask me that?

Adverbs of Frequency: Always, Generally, Never
An adverb of frequency is a word that tells us how frequently an event happens.

Adverbs of frequency represent different percentages of regularity. The adverb never, for example, means that an action happens 0% and the adverb always expresses 100% of the times.

 

When you use adverbs of frequency, you need to consider the position of the verbs.

For any verb different from to be, this is the structure you use:

 Subject+ adverbs of frequency+ verb+ complement

 

For example:

We always send information in the morning

 

However, when the main verb of the sentence is the verb to be you follow another structure:

 Subject+ verb to be +adverbs of frequency + complement

 For example:

We are always in time for the meetings with the manager.

Alyson: Robin, I'm finishing the last details for next week's presentation. Did you prepare your part on values and types?
Robin: Why do you ask me that? You know I am never ready! Can we have a little review before?
Alyson: Sure, I'll go first. What's a data type?
Robin: A data type is a set of values together with a set of operations.
Alyson: Correct! And don't forget what the professor told us last class about the declarative model. It always has a well-defined set of types or basic types.
Robin: Thanks for reminding me of that. I always forget important details! Now, we can also say that programs can calculate with integers or records.
Alyson: Yes, that's right! I have another question. When we have any attempt to use an operation with values, and there is a mistake, the system calculates options and raises an error condition. Why does it happen?

Robin: Because all uses of types are checked. It's impossible for a program to continue when it detects a mistake, so the program never behaves outside of the model; for instance, it hardly ever crashes due to unclear operations on the internal data structures, and it rarely raises an error condition, but it could happen.
Alyson: I'm checking here some specific information related to basic types.
Robin: Yes, I checked that yesterday and I found that the basic types of the declarative model contain numbers which have integers and floats, records which include atoms, booleans, tuples, lists, strings, and also procedures.

Alyson: But those are not all. I could also identify other elements such us chunks, functors, cells, dictionaries, arrays, ports, classes, and objects. Do you think we have to say all of this during the presentation?
Robin: Of course. And don't forget the dynamic typing.
Alyson: Oh, yes! We can mention the two basic approaches to typing. I found those are dynamic and static typing.
Robin: Let me say that part. I made a chart to compare them. Well, I understood that there is a compiler which tries to verify that all operations use values of the correct type…
Alyson: That is the case of the static typing.
Robin: Right! See? You're more than ready. I told you, you need to be more confident!
Alyson: I know…
